title: The Goodness of the Son
english: Through another writing the solution was provided. The new [writing] no longer speaks as in shadow and veil, but clearly and explicitly, as these testify: Paul, writing to the Romans: 'if indeed God is one' (Rom 3:30), and to the Galatians and Corinthians: 'God is one' (Gal 3:28; 1 Cor 8:6). And again to the Corinthians the second [thing]: 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the communion of the Holy Spirit with all of you' (1 Cor 13:13).

Here, because of the sameness of divinity, he first mentioned the Son, and so the Father, then his own Holy Spirit. And he spoke of the communion of the Holy Spirit with Father and Son of the one divinity and glory and kingship. For what other communion is there upon God? To the Ephesians: 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all' (Eph 4:4-6). Then to the same: 'for this reason I bend my knees to the God and Father, from whom every family is named in the heavens and on earth, so that I may give to you, according to the wealth of his glory, power to be strengthened through his own Spirit, so that the Christ may dwell in the inner man through faith in the hearts' (Eph 3:16-17).

Thus again, similarly, because of the equal dignity of the hypostases, after the Father, he first mentioned the Spirit and so the Son. And again to the Corinthians: 'I urge you also, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to contend with me in the prayers to God' (2 Cor 1:11).

And to the Hebrews: 'if indeed the word spoken through angels became firm, and every transgression and disobedience received just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which having begun to speak through the Lord, was made firm to us by those having heard, God co-testifying with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will' (Heb 2:2-4).

Through the Lord, therefore, the Son has been revealed, and through God the Father, and then also the self-determining and almighty Holy Spirit. And the Son showed the one divinity by saying: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God' (Mark 10:18), [and] the three equal and equal-powered [hypostases]...

The argument continues through the teaching regarding baptism. In 18.36, by not saying 'do not call me good' in a testing manner to the legalist, but asking 'why do you call me good?', he showed that he himself is good equal to the Father, and his goodness shines forth from the Father's goodness, being shown to be good having been born from the Good.

In 18.37, 'For if you know me to be good,' he says, 'do not entangle the teacher with the word' like 'Well done, good servant' (Luke 12:42), and like 'The good man brings good out of the good treasure of the heart' (Luke 6:45), and like 'Samuel was good with God and men' (1 Sam 2:26), and 'Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, was better than all Israel by a head and above' (1 Sam 9:2), and 'The good dog lives above the dead lion' (Eccl 9:4). 'Do not withdraw from the primary Good, but recognize me as God, not another in the divinity of the Father, but in the hypostasis.'

In 18.38, for the divinity of both is one; since the first is no longer found to be a single good. 'For it was once read,' he says, 'as "It is good for you to trust in the Lord or to trust in man"' (Ps 31:23). 'For to cling to God is good.' And 'I urged you always to follow me as good and to walk after me' (Luke 9:23).

In 18.39, therefore he did not say 'No one is good except one, the Father', but 'No one is good except one, God', just as in another place he says 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do my words?' (Luke 6:46).

In 18.40, for creation, he says, has goodness by participation, imitating, if it is permitted to say, the innate and perfect goodness of God and being saved through it. And there is an existence of that which has goodness in itself, participating in the goodness of God, clinging to Him through obedience and through love toward Him.
In 18.41, for it was written 'Those who distance themselves from you shall perish' (Ps 145:5), and 'God is far from the ungodly' (Ps 5:5), and 'Salvation is far from sinners' (Ps 34:16).
In 18.42, it is clear that this is in relation and disposition through the opposition toward the good and the degree toward virtue, but not in place.

In 18.43, since he himself is also good, being one by nature with the Good Father, he himself says in Matthew, 'Or is your eye evil because I am good?' (Matt 6:22); and again, 'Mary chose the good portion, which shall not be taken from her' (Luke 10:42). And he said 'the good portion'.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Scriptural Proofs for the Trinity
english: Himself. And they preach by the Spirit. They are not visible men, but they have conversed greatly with the divine Spirit. And these are among the others of their company: the Psalmist in a certain Psalm says: 'Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good' (Ps 106:1). And in the same: 'Let all who fear the Lord say, that He is good' (Ps 135:3). And Jeremiah lamented: 'The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul seeking Him' (Lam 3:25). And Isaiah: 'The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel' (Isa 30:18).

Because also the Holy Spirit of God is good, the one mentioned by David in Psalm 143 sings: 'Your good Spirit shall lead me in a level land' (Ps 143:10). In addition to these, if the eternal life and the words of the Son are good—for He said: 'I am the life' (John 14:6), and again: 'The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and are life' (John 6:64)—and if the sanctification of the Holy Spirit and the energy in the illumination are good (for it is remembered as a co-worker), and also the distribution of the heavenly gifts, then the Son and the Holy Spirit are in every way good.

We were not taught by hearing alone, but we have also seen how the distinct properties of the hypostases of the incorrupt and consubstantial Trinity enter in: of the Father from heaven saying: 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17), of His Only-begotten being baptized on earth, and of His one and only Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon Him, the Only-begotten God and Son. For a Davidic treasure is confirmed in this Psalm, that the one incarnated from among our wombs was attested as Son by God the Father. And the word is known to all, having here: 'Truth has risen up from the earth, righteousness has bowed down from the heavens' (Ps 85:11).

Likewise, because there is no difference in deity, the words sometimes manifest the Father with the Son in the awesome and unblemished Trinity, as when David says: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand' (Ps 110:1), and Paul: 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Rom 1:7). And sometimes they join the Father with the Holy Spirit, as when Haggai prophesies: 'For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, and my Spirit has stood in the midst' (Hag 2:4).

"of you", and again: "not in great power nor in strength, but in my spirit," says the Lord Almighty (Zechariah 4:6). It must be applied to the word. For since the heretics, while the Spirit is being mentioned with the Father, claim that an unsubstantial power is being shown, the preceding word stands securely. And Isaiah: "and now the Lord has sent me and his spirit" (Isaiah 11:3); and again: "there the deer met and gave each other their faces. In number they came, and not one of them perished. The one did not seek the other, because the Lord commanded them and his spirit gathered them together" (Isaiah 65:23).

And Paul to the Corinthians: "do you not know that you are the temple of God and the spirit of God dwells in you" (1 Corinthians 3:16), and again: "the love of God is poured out in your hearts through the holy spirit" (Romans 5:5), and again: "but God has revealed to us through his spirit" (1 Corinthians 2:10). At other times they name only the Son, as when Isaiah prophesies: "and now, Lord, you are our Father, and we are all works of clay of your hands" (Isaiah 64:8); and Paul to the Galatians: "for as many as were baptized into Christ, have clothed themselves with Christ" (Galatians 3:27).

At other times they proclaim the only-begotten with the holy spirit, as when Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11), to the Romans: "I say the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the holy spirit" (Romans 2:15), and again: "for if indeed the one coming preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit, which you did not receive" (2 Corinthians 11:4).

And at other times he reminds us of the holy spirit, as when Isaiah prophesies: "they rebelled and provoked the holy spirit" (Isaiah 63:10), and again: "a spirit came down from the Lord and led them" (Isaiah 48:16); and Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but a natural man does not receive the things of the spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). And just as Stephen declares in the Acts: "you resist the holy spirit" (Acts 7:51), and again: "we are witnesses of these words and the holy spirit" (Acts 22:52), just as we have become accustomed to say: "we alone are here and God [is also]."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of the Trinity and the Vision of Isaiah
english: And the Savior alone mentions the divine Spirit according to John, saying: 'But when He comes, that Spirit of truth, He will guide you into all the truth' (John 16:13).

And the deeds likewise testify to this: 'And while Peter was deliberating concerning the word, the Holy Spirit said to him, Stand up, go down, and walk with them without any hesitation, because I have sent them' (Acts 10:19); and again: 'These things the Holy Spirit says: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work, whom I have called' (Acts 13:2); and again the Holy Spirit said to Peter: 'Stand up, go' (Acts 10:33) to the house of Cornelius.

And again the apostolic deeds, being elegant, provide a demonstration by such a word; for they contain: 'Then Paul, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, said to him' (Acts 13:9), and also: 'For Peter, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, said to the people' (Acts 11:5).

Similarly, the equal-balance and equal-power of the all-divine hypostases is signified, and in the Word, the Lord God, through His most-praised voice having been foretold for the baptism, the equal-honor to Himself and to the Holy Spirit for keeping [the relation] toward the Father; through which the holy books sometimes first mention the Father and thus the Son or the Holy Spirit, and sometimes first remember the Son because of the indivisibility of nature and the indistinguishability of theology; as when Job declares the Trinity boldly: 'The Lord lives, who has thus judged me, and the Almighty, who has afflicted my soul; indeed, my breath is still remaining, but a divine spirit surrounds me in my nostrils' (Job 5:14). He says [that He is] the one making alive with a Holy Spirit and still breathing, making [it] so.

And as when Paul writes to the Thessalonians the second time: 'And our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God and Father will exhort your hearts' (1 Thess 3:11), and to the Galatians: 'Paul, an apostle, not from man nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father' (Gal 1:1), and to the Corinthians, as is previously stated: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit' (2 Cor 13:13).
And the Savior says: 'We will come, I and the Father, and we will make a dwelling with Him alone' (John 14:21).

First they name the Holy Spirit, and then the Father or the Son, as when David sings: 'Where shall I go from your spirit, and from your face where shall I flee?' (Ps 139:7). And Job, showing his good conscience, says: 'A divine spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me' (Job 32:8). And as Paul writes in the first epistle to the Corinthians: 'There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and diversities of operations, but the same God who works all in all' (1 Cor 12:4-6). Sometimes they speak homonymously concerning two hypostases, as when Zechariah says: 'The Lord said to the devil: The Lord will rebuke you, devil' (Zech 3:1). And it was shown more clearly through many [examples].

Concerning what has now been said about the Father, sometimes it is said about the Son or about the Holy Spirit because the Trinity exists in one divinity. In one single divinity, the hierophants, knowing the glorious Trinity and its theology being common, sometimes speak about the Father, sometimes others about the Son or about the Holy Spirit, not opposing one another, but because we also know this very thing to be the opportune part of the right faith; and just as whatever hypostasis we remember from everything, we also received the other with faith, as inseparable.

But it is necessary for the truthful ones, who deny the truth of glory, to be truthful in teaching the simple and truly true, that is, the goodness of God. For they say it is not right for the impure to touch the pure; but those were pure and strangers to all false glory. And we shall find this immediately in the theophany which Isaiah saw. And why not first [mention] the whole of that place as it is?

So he says: 'I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the house was full of his glory. And seraphim were standing around him; six wings to the one and six wings to the one; with two wings they covered the faces, with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and one was crying to another: Holy, holy' (Isa 6:1-3).
